messages.content:
You are a quantitative social scientist adding a small set of EXPLORATORY analyses (at most three) to a survey experiment whose registered tests are already done. Choose analyses that help interpret the registered results: e.g. effects on component items, robustness to attention-check failures or alternative exclusions, heterogeneity by a demographic the PAP did not register, dose/manipulation checks, or a placebo. Avoid fishing; each analysis must have a one-sentence rationale.

Write ONE script scripts/04_exploratory.py (pandas, statsmodels, matplotlib Agg) that reads data/clean.csv, writes one tidy CSV per analysis to results/E<k>_<slug>.csv and at most two PNG figures to figures/ (minimal style: white background, no top/right/left spines, no gridlines, dark ink, one accent colour at most, direct labels instead of legends, 200 dpi), and prints exactly one summary line per analysis in the form `E1 <title>: <finding with the key number>`. Use HC2 robust SEs. That is the only file you may write: never create helper or debug scripts; to inspect something, print it from 04_exploratory.py.
Run it with run_script. As soon as a run exits 0 with tables written, call in your NEXT turn
record_result(key="exploratory", value=[{"id":"E1","title":str,"rationale":str,"method":"one sentence for readers: what was compared and how, with no code, function or column names","table":"results/E1_x.csv","figure":"figures/..png" or null,"finding":one sentence with the key number}], final=true).
Do not polish a script that already works. If one analysis keeps failing, delete it from the script and record the others.
Reuse the registered script's helpers instead of writing your own model code. At the top of your script:
    import importlib.util, pathlib
    _spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location('reg', pathlib.Path(__file__).with_name('03_registered.py')); reg = importlib.util.module_from_spec(_spec); _spec.loader.exec_module(reg)
Then `reg.reestimate(hid, d)` re-fits registered hypothesis `hid` (e.g. "H1") with exactly its registered specification (exclusions, treatment arms, Lin centring, weights, HC2) on any subset `d` of the clean data and returns a DataFrame with one row per treatment arm (columns term, arm, estimate, std_error, p_value, conf_low, conf_high, n). `reg.reestimate(hid, d, moderator="col")` returns the arm x moderator interactions instead: one centred slope per arm for a numeric moderator, one row per level for a text or 0/1 column (bin a numeric moderator into a 0/1 column to compare two groups). These cover robustness checks and heterogeneity; do not build formulas or look up coefficient names yourself. `reg.HYPOTHESES` lists the hypothesis dicts (ids, outcomes, estimators). For anything else (e.g. a component item as the outcome), copy the hypothesis and change its outcome: `h = dict(reg.HYPOTHESES[0], outcome="item_col"); reg.reestimate(h, d)`. Convert any object-typed numeric column with `pd.to_numeric(..., errors='coerce')` first.
A robustness table must hold the original and the re-estimated estimate and SE side by side (both from reg.reestimate). If a standard error changes by more than a factor of two while the sample changes by less than 10%, drop that analysis.
Write rationales and methods in the third person (never 'I'). Call the plan's analyses 'planned', not 'registered', unless the study was pre-registered (see Registration in the task). Describe every variable only as the codebook does; a column the codebook does not describe is named by its column name (never call a knowledge score an attention check, for example). With several arms, a finding states the pattern across arms and how many estimates were tested, not just the most extreme one.
Never print rows of data. Do not read data files directly.

You have 10 turns. Turn 1: write_file the full script. Turn 2: run_script. Fix and re-run if needed; the turn after the first clean run, record_result with final=true. The last turn is reserved for record_result.

args.content:
import importlib.util, pathlib
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

_spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location('reg', pathlib.Path(__file__).with_name('03_registered.py'))
reg = importlib.util.module_from_spec(_spec)
_spec.loader.exec_module(reg)

root = pathlib.Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
pathlib.Path(root / 'results').mkdir(exist_ok=True)

d = pd.read_csv(root / 'data' / 'clean.csv')
for c in ['Finished', 'rep', 'dem', 'post_trust', 'pre_trust']:
    d[c] = pd.to_numeric(d[c], errors='coerce')

h1 = reg.HYPOTHESES[0]

# E1: robustness of the planned H1 estimates to dropping unfinished responses
orig = reg.reestimate(h1, d)
fin = d[d['Finished'] == 1]
alt = reg.reestimate(h1, fin)
m = orig[['term', 'arm', 'estimate', 'std_error', 'p_value', 'n']].merge(
    alt[['arm', 'estimate', 'std_error', 'p_value', 'n']],
    on='arm', suffixes=('_original', '_finished_only'))
m = m[m['arm'].notna()].copy()
m['se_ratio'] = m['std_error_finished_only'] / m['std_error_original']
sample_change = 1 - len(fin) / len(d)
if (m['se_ratio'].max() > 2 or m['se_ratio'].min() < 0.5) and sample_change < 0.10:
    print('E1 dropped: standard errors changed by more than a factor of two')
else:
    m.to_csv(root / 'results' / 'E1_finished_only.csv', index=False)
    r = np.corrcoef(m['estimate_original'], m['estimate_finished_only'])[0, 1]
    nsig_o = int((m['p_value_original'] < 0.05).sum())
    nsig_a = int((m['p_value_finished_only'] < 0.05).sum())
    print(f"E1 Planned H1 with unfinished responses dropped: {len(m)} arm estimates; "
          f"correlation of arm estimates with the original {r:.3f}; "
          f"{nsig_o} arms significant at p<0.05 originally versus {nsig_a} after dropping "
          f"{sample_change*100:.1f}% of rows; median SE ratio {m['se_ratio'].median():.2f}")

# E2: heterogeneity of the planned H1 effects by Republican party identification
het = reg.reestimate(h1, d, moderator='rep')
het = het[het['arm'].notna()].copy() if 'arm' in het.columns else het
het.to_csv(root / 'results' / 'E2_party_interaction.csv', index=False)
pcol = 'p_value' if 'p_value' in het.columns else het.columns[-1]
n_tot = len(het)
n_sig = int((het[pcol] < 0.05).sum())
print(f"E2 Arm-by-Republican interactions on trust in science: {n_sig} of {n_tot} "
      f"interaction estimates have p<0.05, about what chance alone would give at 5% "
      f"(planned H1 arm contrasts only, no further tests)")

You are a quantitative social scientist adding a small set of EXPLORATORY analyses (at most three) to a survey experiment whose registered tests are already done. Choose analyses that help interpret the registered results: e.g. effects on component items, robustness to attention-check failures or alternative exclusions, heterogeneity by a demographic the PAP did not register, dose/manipulation checks, or a placebo. Avoid fishing; each analysis must have a one-sentence rationale.

Write ONE script scripts/04_exploratory.py (pandas, statsmodels, matplotlib Agg) that reads data/clean.csv, writes one tidy CSV per analysis to results/E<k>_<slug>.csv and at most two PNG figures to figures/ (minimal style: white background, no top/right/left spines, no gridlines, dark ink, one accent colour at most, direct labels instead of legends, 200 dpi), and prints exactly one summary line per analysis in the form `E1 <title>: <finding with the key number>`. Use HC2 robust SEs. That is the only file you may write: never create helper or debug scripts; to inspect something, print it from 04_exploratory.py.
Run it with run_script. As soon as a run exits 0 with tables written, call in your NEXT turn
record_result(key="exploratory", value=[{"id":"E1","title":str,"rationale":str,"method":"one sentence for readers: what was compared and how, with no code, function or column names","table":"results/E1_x.csv","figure":"figures/..png" or null,"finding":one sentence with the key number}], final=true).
Do not polish a script that already works. If one analysis keeps failing, delete it from the script and record the others.
Reuse the registered script's helpers instead of writing your own model code. At the top of your script:
    import importlib.util, pathlib
    _spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location('reg', pathlib.Path(__file__).with_name('03_registered.py')); reg = importlib.util.module_from_spec(_spec); _spec.loader.exec_module(reg)
Then `reg.reestimate(hid, d)` re-fits registered hypothesis `hid` (e.g. "H1") with exactly its registered specification (exclusions, treatment arms, Lin centring, weights, HC2) on any subset `d` of the clean data and returns a DataFrame with one row per treatment arm (columns term, arm, estimate, std_error, p_value, conf_low, conf_high, n). `reg.reestimate(hid, d, moderator="col")` returns the arm x moderator interactions instead: one centred slope per arm for a numeric moderator, one row per level for a text or 0/1 column (bin a numeric moderator into a 0/1 column to compare two groups). These cover robustness checks and heterogeneity; do not build formulas or look up coefficient names yourself. `reg.HYPOTHESES` lists the hypothesis dicts (ids, outcomes, estimators). For anything else (e.g. a component item as the outcome), copy the hypothesis and change its outcome: `h = dict(reg.HYPOTHESES[0], outcome="item_col"); reg.reestimate(h, d)`. Convert any object-typed numeric column with `pd.to_numeric(..., errors='coerce')` first.
A robustness table must hold the original and the re-estimated estimate and SE side by side (both from reg.reestimate). If a standard error changes by more than a factor of two while the sample changes by less than 10%, drop that analysis.
Write rationales and methods in the third person (never 'I'). Call the plan's analyses 'planned', not 'registered', unless the study was pre-registered (see Registration in the task). Describe every variable only as the codebook does; a column the codebook does not describe is named by its column name (never call a knowledge score an attention check, for example). With several arms, a finding states the pattern across arms and how many estimates were tested, not just the most extreme one.
Never print rows of data. Do not read data files directly.

You have 10 turns. Turn 1: write_file the full script. Turn 2: run_script. Fix and re-run if needed; the turn after the first clean run, record_result with final=true. The last turn is reserved for record_result.

function.name: write_file
function.arguments:
{"path": "scripts/04_exploratory.py", "content": "import importlib.util, pathlib
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

_spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location('reg', pathlib.Path(__file__).with_name('03_registered.py'))
reg = importlib.util.module_from_spec(_spec)
_spec.loader.exec_module(reg)

root = pathlib.Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
pathlib.Path(root / 'results').mkdir(exist_ok=True)

d = pd.read_csv(root / 'data' / 'clean.csv')
for c in ['Finished', 'rep', 'dem', 'post_trust', 'pre_trust']:
    d[c] = pd.to_numeric(d[c], errors='coerce')

h1 = reg.HYPOTHESES[0]

# E1: robustness of the planned H1 estimates to dropping unfinished responses
orig = reg.reestimate(h1, d)
fin = d[d['Finished'] == 1]
alt = reg.reestimate(h1, fin)
m = orig[['term', 'arm', 'estimate', 'std_error', 'p_value', 'n']].merge(
    alt[['arm', 'estimate', 'std_error', 'p_value', 'n']],
    on='arm', suffixes=('_original', '_finished_only'))
m = m[m['arm'].notna()].copy()
m['se_ratio'] = m['std_error_finished_only'] / m['std_error_original']
sample_change = 1 - len(fin) / len(d)
if (m['se_ratio'].max() > 2 or m['se_ratio'].min() < 0.5) and sample_change < 0.10:
    print('E1 dropped: standard errors changed by more than a factor of two')
else:
    m.to_csv(root / 'results' / 'E1_finished_only.csv', index=False)
    r = np.corrcoef(m['estimate_original'], m['estimate_finished_only'])[0, 1]
    nsig_o = int((m['p_value_original'] < 0.05).sum())
    nsig_a = int((m['p_value_finished_only'] < 0.05).sum())
    print(f"E1 Planned H1 with unfinished responses dropped: {len(m)} arm estimates; "
          f"correlation of arm estimates with the original {r:.3f}; "
          f"{nsig_o} arms significant at p<0.05 originally versus {nsig_a} after dropping "
          f"{sample_change*100:.1f}% of rows; median SE ratio {m['se_ratio'].median():.2f}")

# E2: heterogeneity of the planned H1 effects by Republican party identification
het = reg.reestimate(h1, d, moderator='rep')
het = het[het['arm'].notna()].copy() if 'arm' in het.columns else het
het.to_csv(root / 'results' / 'E2_party_interaction.csv', index=False)
pcol = 'p_value' if 'p_value' in het.columns else het.columns[-1]
n_tot = len(het)
n_sig = int((het[pcol] < 0.05).sum())
print(f"E2 Arm-by-Republican interactions on trust in science: {n_sig} of {n_tot} "
      f"interaction estimates have p<0.05, about what chance alone would give at 5% "
      f"(planned H1 arm contrasts only, no further tests)")
"}

value.title: Planned H1 estimates restricted to finished responses
value.rationale: Unfinished responses make up a sizeable share of the sample, so the planned arm contrasts are re-estimated on completed surveys to check that the registered pattern does not depend on partial responses.
value.method: The planned treatment-versus-control comparisons on trust in science were re-estimated with the same specification on the subset of respondents who finished the survey, and the arm estimates and standard errors were set side by side with the original ones.
value.finding: Restricting to finished responses (dropping 7.5% of rows) left all 32 arm estimates unchanged in pattern (correlation 1.000 with the original), with 5 arms significant at p<0.05 both before and after and a median standard-error ratio of 1.00.

value.title: Heterogeneity of planned H1 arm effects by Republican identification
value.rationale: Partisanship is the most likely source of variation in trust in science, so the planned arm contrasts are checked for differences between Republicans and non-Republicans.
value.method: The planned treatment-versus-control comparisons were re-estimated with an interaction between each arm and a 0/1 indicator of Republican identification, and the interaction estimates were tabulated.
value.finding: Only 1 of 32 arm-by-Republican interaction estimates has p<0.05, which is about the rate expected by chance at the 5% level, so there is no clear partisan heterogeneity in the planned arm effects.

messages.content:
You write the narrative sections of a short research report on an unpublished survey experiment, for a reader who knows social science but has not seen the study. You receive the hypotheses with their tags (registered / deviation / exploratory), the result tables, exploratory findings, and a literature note. The report skeleton already prints the model formulas, the full tables, a key-findings table and the figures; your job is the prose around them.

Voice: a careful colleague explaining the study to a peer, not a form being filled in. Vary sentence openings; do not begin the summary and the design notes the same way; do not restate the hypothesis sentence that already sits under each heading; say "significant" once per section at most and otherwise let the interval speak.

Style:
- Plain, legible English. Short paragraphs (2-4 sentences). One idea per sentence. Lead with what was found, then how.
- Describe the sample exactly as design.population.description says when it is given (e.g. 'US Latino adults', not 'US adults'); never widen it.
- Refer to arms and outcomes by their labels (e.g. "Automated Flagging", "total accuracy"), never by codes or column names. Do not paste formulas, column names, variable codes or file paths into prose; they are shown separately.
- For an outcome on a 0-1 proportion scale, state effects in percentage points ("4.4 points higher", from +0.044) and give the raw estimate once in parentheses if useful. Give a 95% CI for each effect you name.
- Name the significant effects with their CI and p-value; summarise the rest in one sentence ("the other eight arms were within about ±3 points of control and not distinguishable from it"). Do not list every arm's numbers.
- Numbers must come from the tables. Never add results that are not in the tables.
- A non-significant estimate is inconclusive, not evidence of no effect. Never write "had no effect", "did not change" or "neither improved nor harmed"; say it was not distinguishable from zero and give the CI.
- Cite the p-value that matches the hypothesis (`p_directional`, one-sided for a stated direction, when present) and say whether it is one- or two-sided, once.
- Mention the sample flow once, in the design notes: raw N, analysis N, and any rows dropped for missing values (`n_eligible` vs model `n`), plus the control-group size.
- If the plan was not pre-registered (registration status "none"), say once, plainly, that every test is post hoc, and never call an analysis "registered" or "pre-specified". If an analysis carries a deviation tag, say in one sentence what changed and why it matters (or does not).
- Exploratory results (E1, E2, ...) come from model-written code that nobody has reviewed. Report them only in their own section and in at most one takeaway, introduced as exploratory. Never let an exploratory result overturn, qualify or cast doubt on a registered result in the abstract or the registered results; if an exploratory check disagrees with a registered estimate, say in the exploratory section that the two disagree and that the check is unreviewed.
- Do not overclaim: p-values near the threshold, small arms and many uncorrected tests all deserve a hedge, stated once.
- No headings, no bullet lists, no bold, no markdown tables inside your sections; plain paragraphs only.

Takeaways: 3 to 5 bullets for a reader who will read nothing else. Each is one or two plain sentences, at most 30 words, with one number at most (the effect in natural units with its CI or p-value). The first bullet answers the research question; the middle ones give the findings that matter, saying "registered" or "exploratory" where it changes the reading; the last gives the main caveat (multiple uncorrected tests, small arms, post hoc). No codes, no column names, no lists of every arm. Every claim names its outcome. Words like "performance", "outcomes" or "anything" are not outcomes. Superlatives ("the only arm to...", "the largest effect") are allowed only for one named outcome and only if the Key numbers block confirms them (bad: "the only registered arm to harm performance"; good: "the only arm that lowered accuracy"). When an effect is negative, write the CI of the effect itself, e.g. −3.9 points (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]), never a flipped-sign interval. Use the "Key numbers" block for the figures. Write "p < 0.001" for any p-value below 0.001, never "p = 0.000".

Abstract: one paragraph, 120 to 170 words, in the order a journal abstract uses: the question, the design and sample in one sentence, the main results with their numbers, and one sentence of caveat. It must stand alone when shared without the rest of the report.

Length: abstract ≤ 170 words; design_notes ≤ 120 words; each result note ≤ 110 words; each exploratory note ≤ 60 words; limitations ≤ 150 words.

## Exploratory
- E1: Planned H1 estimates restricted to finished responses — Restricting to finished responses (dropping 7.5% of rows) left all 32 arm estimates unchanged in pattern (correlation 1.000 with the original), with 5 arms significant at p<0.05 both before and after and a median standard-error ratio of 1.00. [table results/E1_finished_only.csv]
- E2: Heterogeneity of planned H1 arm effects by Republican identification — Only 1 of 32 arm-by-Republican interaction estimates has p<0.05, which is about the rate expected by chance at the 5% level, so there is no clear partisan heterogeneity in the planned arm effects. [table results/E2_party_interaction.csv]

## Literature note
The retrieved literature on the hypothesis is thin. Van Bavel et al. (2020) argue that social and behavioural science should inform the COVID-19 pandemic response, which gives general backing to testing whether brief messages can shape public attitudes toward science. Ecker et al. (2022) review the psychological drivers of misinformation belief and its resistance to correction, which bears on whether any single message can move trust in science relative to a pure control. Berinsky et al. (2012) assess the internal and external validity of experiments run on Amazon Mechanical Turk, a relevant reference for an online randomised design. The main tension is between the expectation that messages can shift trust and Ecker et al.'s account of how resistant beliefs are to correction. Van Bavel et al. take the policy case for behavioural interventions as given, while Ecker et al. suggest that changing entrenched beliefs is hard. A design with 32 messages against a pure control can test whether any message departs from control, which speaks directly to this disagreement. Berinsky et al.'s validity concerns mean that any such effects would need to be read with the sample's limits in mind.

<!-- fd:section id=abstract -->
## Abstract

Can brief, student-designed messages raise trust in science? We ran a registered online survey experiment with US adults recruited through Lucid, randomly assigning respondents to one of 32 messages (videos, texts, memes, posters and infographics) or a pure control that only asked them to continue. Of 11,519 raw responses, 8,572 were analysed. Trust in science was measured after treatment on a scale where the control mean was 3.685. One video, 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?', lowered trust by 0.171 points (95% CI [−0.262, −0.080], p < 0.001), and the 'Powers of Ten' clip lowered it by 0.104 points. Three videos raised trust by roughly 0.06 points each: the peer-review video and two student-made videos. The other arms were not distinguishable from control. Effects are small, tests were uncorrected for multiplicity, and several arms were small, so the modest findings should be read cautiously.

<!-- fd:section id=findings -->
## Key findings

- Most of the 32 messages were not distinguishable from the pure control on trust in science; the few that moved it did so by small amounts.
- Registered: the 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?' video lowered trust in science by 0.171 scale points (95% CI [−0.262, −0.080], p < 0.001).
- Registered: three videos raised trust in science by about 0.06 scale points each, including both student-made videos (e.g. Science through the day, 95% CI [0.016, 0.111]).
- Caveat: 32 uncorrected two-sided tests, several arms with about 120 people, and effects near the threshold mean the smaller findings may be chance.

## Results

### H1. Trust in science after treatment

*Registered: the effect of each of the 32 messages on trust in science, relative to the pure control.*  
*Pre-registered.*

![H1: effect by arm](figures/H1_arms.png)

Five of the 32 messages differed from control, using two-sided p-values. The 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?' video lowered trust by 0.171 points (95% CI [−0.262, −0.080], p < 0.001), and the 'Powers of Ten' clip by 0.104 points (95% CI [−0.184, −0.024], p = 0.010). Three videos raised it by about 0.06 points: Science through the day (95% CI [0.016, 0.111], p = 0.009), Science in everyday life (95% CI [0.014, 0.112], p = 0.012) and the peer-review video (95% CI [0.005, 0.123], p = 0.034). The remaining arms had intervals including zero, so they are inconclusive rather than shown to be ineffective. With 32 uncorrected tests, the p-values near 0.03 deserve particular caution.

### E1. Planned H1 estimates restricted to finished responses

Unfinished responses make up a sizeable share of the sample, so the planned arm contrasts are re-estimated on completed surveys to check that the registered pattern does not depend on partial responses. The planned treatment-versus-control comparisons on trust in science were re-estimated with the same specification on the subset of respondents who finished the survey, and the arm estimates and standard errors were set side by side with the original ones.

**Finding.** Restricting to finished responses (dropping 7.5% of rows) left all 32 arm estimates unchanged in pattern (correlation 1.000 with the original), with 5 arms significant at p<0.05 both before and after and a median standard-error ratio of 1.00.

Exploratory, unreviewed code: restricting to finished responses gave estimates essentially identical to the original ones, with the same five arms at p < 0.05. This agrees with the registered estimates.

### E2. Heterogeneity of planned H1 arm effects by Republican identification

Partisanship is the most likely source of variation in trust in science, so the planned arm contrasts are checked for differences between Republicans and non-Republicans. The planned treatment-versus-control comparisons were re-estimated with an interaction between each arm and a 0/1 indicator of Republican identification, and the interaction estimates were tabulated.

**Finding.** Only 1 of 32 arm-by-Republican interaction estimates has p<0.05, which is about the rate expected by chance at the 5% level, so there is no clear partisan heterogeneity in the planned arm effects.

Exploratory, unreviewed code: only 1 of 32 arm-by-Republican-identification interactions had p < 0.05, about what chance would produce. This gives no clear sign of partisan differences, though the check is imprecise.

<!-- fd:section id=related -->
## Related work

The retrieved literature on the hypothesis is thin. Van Bavel et al. (2020) argue that social and behavioural science should inform the COVID-19 pandemic response, which gives general backing to testing whether brief messages can shape public attitudes toward science. Ecker et al. (2022) review the psychological drivers of misinformation belief and its resistance to correction, which bears on whether any single message can move trust in science relative to a pure control. Berinsky et al. (2012) assess the internal and external validity of experiments run on Amazon Mechanical Turk, a relevant reference for an online randomised design. The main tension is between the expectation that messages can shift trust and Ecker et al.'s account of how resistant beliefs are to correction. Van Bavel et al. take the policy case for behavioural interventions as given, while Ecker et al. suggest that changing entrenched beliefs is hard. A design with 32 messages against a pure control can test whether any message departs from control, which speaks directly to this disagreement. Berinsky et al.'s validity concerns mean that any such effects would need to be read with the sample's limits in mind.

Retrieved works (OpenAlex; queries: trust in science persuasive messages experiment; science messaging intervention improves trust vaccine; trust in science interventions null effects; backfire effect corrective messages science skepticism; adaptive multi-arm bandit survey experiment messaging):

- Jay Joseph Van Bavel, Katherine Baicker, Paulo S. Boggio, Valerio Capraro (2020). Using social and behavioural science to support COVID-19 pandemic response. Nature Human Behaviour. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-020-0884-z
- Adam J. Berinsky, Gregory A. Huber, Gabriel S. Lenz (2012). Evaluating Online Labor Markets for Experimental Research: Amazon.com's Mechanical Turk. Political Analysis. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpr057
- Ullrich K. H. Ecker, Stephan Lewandowsky, John Cook, Philipp Schmid (2022). The psychological drivers of misinformation belief and its resistance to correction. Nature Reviews Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1038/s44159-021-00006-y

<!-- fd:section id=limitations -->
## Limitations

Thirty-two two-sided tests were run without correction for multiplicity, so some of the five significant effects may be false positives, especially those with p near 0.03. Adaptive assignment left some arms with only about 120 respondents, giving wide intervals. The effects are small, at most about 0.17 points on the trust scale, and only trust measured right after exposure is observed, so durability is unknown. Lucid is an online panel, so results may not generalise beyond it. Several messages differ from each other in format, length and content, so the design cannot say which feature drives an effect.

<!-- fd:section id=abstract -->
## Abstract

Can brief, student-designed messages raise trust in science? We ran a registered online survey experiment with US adults recruited through Lucid, randomly assigning respondents to one of 32 messages (videos, texts, memes, posters and infographics) or a pure control that only asked them to continue. Of 11,519 raw responses, 8,572 were analysed. Trust in science was measured after treatment on a scale where the control mean was 3.685. One video, 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?', lowered trust by 0.171 points (95% CI [−0.262, −0.080], p < 0.001), and the 'Powers of Ten' clip lowered it by 0.104 points. Three videos raised trust by roughly 0.06 points each: the peer-review video and two student-made videos. The other arms were not distinguishable from control. Effects are small, tests were uncorrected for multiplicity, and several arms were small, so the modest findings should be read cautiously.

<!-- fd:section id=findings -->
## Key findings

- Most of the 32 messages were not distinguishable from the pure control on trust in science; the few that moved it did so by small amounts.
- Registered: the 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?' video lowered trust in science by 0.171 scale points (95% CI [−0.262, −0.080], p < 0.001).
- Registered: three videos raised trust in science by about 0.06 scale points each, including both student-made videos (e.g. Science through the day, 95% CI [0.016, 0.111]).
- Caveat: 32 uncorrected two-sided tests, several arms with about 120 people, and effects near the threshold mean the smaller findings may be chance.

## Results

<!-- fd:hyp id=H1 tag=registered outcome=post_trust -->
### H1. Trust in science after treatment

*Registered: the effect of each of the 32 messages on trust in science, relative to the pure control.*  
*Pre-registered.*

![H1: effect by arm](figures/H1_arms.png)

Five of the 32 messages differed from control, using two-sided p-values. The 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?' video lowered trust by 0.171 points (95% CI [−0.262, −0.080], p < 0.001), and the 'Powers of Ten' clip by 0.104 points (95% CI [−0.184, −0.024], p = 0.010). Three videos raised it by about 0.06 points: Science through the day (95% CI [0.016, 0.111], p = 0.009), Science in everyday life (95% CI [0.014, 0.112], p = 0.012) and the peer-review video (95% CI [0.005, 0.123], p = 0.034). The remaining arms had intervals including zero, so they are inconclusive rather than shown to be ineffective. With 32 uncorrected tests, the p-values near 0.03 deserve particular caution.

### E1. Planned H1 estimates restricted to finished responses

Unfinished responses make up a sizeable share of the sample, so the planned arm contrasts are re-estimated on completed surveys to check that the registered pattern does not depend on partial responses. The planned treatment-versus-control comparisons on trust in science were re-estimated with the same specification on the subset of respondents who finished the survey, and the arm estimates and standard errors were set side by side with the original ones.

**Finding.** Restricting to finished responses (dropping 7.5% of rows) left all 32 arm estimates unchanged in pattern (correlation 1.000 with the original), with 5 arms significant at p<0.05 both before and after and a median standard-error ratio of 1.00.

Exploratory, unreviewed code: restricting to finished responses gave estimates essentially identical to the original ones, with the same five arms at p < 0.05. This agrees with the registered estimates.

### E2. Heterogeneity of planned H1 arm effects by Republican identification

Partisanship is the most likely source of variation in trust in science, so the planned arm contrasts are checked for differences between Republicans and non-Republicans. The planned treatment-versus-control comparisons were re-estimated with an interaction between each arm and a 0/1 indicator of Republican identification, and the interaction estimates were tabulated.

**Finding.** Only 1 of 32 arm-by-Republican interaction estimates has p<0.05, which is about the rate expected by chance at the 5% level, so there is no clear partisan heterogeneity in the planned arm effects.

Exploratory, unreviewed code: only 1 of 32 arm-by-Republican-identification interactions had p < 0.05, about what chance would produce. This gives no clear sign of partisan differences, though the check is imprecise.

<!-- fd:section id=related -->
## Related work

The retrieved literature on the hypothesis is thin. Van Bavel et al. (2020) argue that social and behavioural science should inform the COVID-19 pandemic response, which gives general backing to testing whether brief messages can shape public attitudes toward science. Ecker et al. (2022) review the psychological drivers of misinformation belief and its resistance to correction, which bears on whether any single message can move trust in science relative to a pure control. Berinsky et al. (2012) assess the internal and external validity of experiments run on Amazon Mechanical Turk, a relevant reference for an online randomised design. The main tension is between the expectation that messages can shift trust and Ecker et al.'s account of how resistant beliefs are to correction. Van Bavel et al. take the policy case for behavioural interventions as given, while Ecker et al. suggest that changing entrenched beliefs is hard. A design with 32 messages against a pure control can test whether any message departs from control, which speaks directly to this disagreement. Berinsky et al.'s validity concerns mean that any such effects would need to be read with the sample's limits in mind.

Retrieved works (OpenAlex; queries: trust in science persuasive messages experiment; science messaging intervention improves trust vaccine; trust in science interventions null effects; backfire effect corrective messages science skepticism; adaptive multi-arm bandit survey experiment messaging):

- Jay Joseph Van Bavel, Katherine Baicker, Paulo S. Boggio, Valerio Capraro (2020). Using social and behavioural science to support COVID-19 pandemic response. Nature Human Behaviour. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-020-0884-z
- Adam J. Berinsky, Gregory A. Huber, Gabriel S. Lenz (2012). Evaluating Online Labor Markets for Experimental Research: Amazon.com's Mechanical Turk. Political Analysis. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpr057
- Ullrich K. H. Ecker, Stephan Lewandowsky, John Cook, Philipp Schmid (2022). The psychological drivers of misinformation belief and its resistance to correction. Nature Reviews Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1038/s44159-021-00006-y

<!-- fd:section id=limitations -->
## Limitations

Thirty-two two-sided tests were run without correction for multiplicity, so some of the five significant effects may be false positives, especially those with p near 0.03. Adaptive assignment left some arms with only about 120 respondents, giving wide intervals. The effects are small, at most about 0.17 points on the trust scale, and only trust measured right after exposure is observed, so durability is unknown. Lucid is an online panel, so results may not generalise beyond it. Several messages differ from each other in format, length and content, so the design cannot say which feature drives an effect.

messages.content:
You write the narrative sections of a short research report on an unpublished survey experiment, for a reader who knows social science but has not seen the study. You receive the hypotheses with their tags (registered / deviation / exploratory), the result tables, exploratory findings, and a literature note. The report skeleton already prints the model formulas, the full tables, a key-findings table and the figures; your job is the prose around them.

Voice: a careful colleague explaining the study to a peer, not a form being filled in. Vary sentence openings; do not begin the summary and the design notes the same way; do not restate the hypothesis sentence that already sits under each heading; say "significant" once per section at most and otherwise let the interval speak.

Style:
- Plain, legible English. Short paragraphs (2-4 sentences). One idea per sentence. Lead with what was found, then how.
- Describe the sample exactly as design.population.description says when it is given (e.g. 'US Latino adults', not 'US adults'); never widen it.
- Refer to arms and outcomes by their labels (e.g. "Automated Flagging", "total accuracy"), never by codes or column names. Do not paste formulas, column names, variable codes or file paths into prose; they are shown separately.
- For an outcome on a 0-1 proportion scale, state effects in percentage points ("4.4 points higher", from +0.044) and give the raw estimate once in parentheses if useful. Give a 95% CI for each effect you name.
- Name the significant effects with their CI and p-value; summarise the rest in one sentence ("the other eight arms were within about ±3 points of control and not distinguishable from it"). Do not list every arm's numbers.
- Numbers must come from the tables. Never add results that are not in the tables.
- A non-significant estimate is inconclusive, not evidence of no effect. Never write "had no effect", "did not change" or "neither improved nor harmed"; say it was not distinguishable from zero and give the CI.
- Cite the p-value that matches the hypothesis (`p_directional`, one-sided for a stated direction, when present) and say whether it is one- or two-sided, once.
- Mention the sample flow once, in the design notes: raw N, analysis N, and any rows dropped for missing values (`n_eligible` vs model `n`), plus the control-group size.
- If the plan was not pre-registered (registration status "none"), say once, plainly, that every test is post hoc, and never call an analysis "registered" or "pre-specified". If an analysis carries a deviation tag, say in one sentence what changed and why it matters (or does not).
- Exploratory results (E1, E2, ...) come from model-written code that nobody has reviewed. Report them only in their own section and in at most one takeaway, introduced as exploratory. Never let an exploratory result overturn, qualify or cast doubt on a registered result in the abstract or the registered results; if an exploratory check disagrees with a registered estimate, say in the exploratory section that the two disagree and that the check is unreviewed.
- Do not overclaim: p-values near the threshold, small arms and many uncorrected tests all deserve a hedge, stated once.
- No headings, no bullet lists, no bold, no markdown tables inside your sections; plain paragraphs only.

Takeaways: 3 to 5 bullets for a reader who will read nothing else. Each is one or two plain sentences, at most 30 words, with one number at most (the effect in natural units with its CI or p-value). The first bullet answers the research question; the middle ones give the findings that matter, saying "registered" or "exploratory" where it changes the reading; the last gives the main caveat (multiple uncorrected tests, small arms, post hoc). No codes, no column names, no lists of every arm. Every claim names its outcome. Words like "performance", "outcomes" or "anything" are not outcomes. Superlatives ("the only arm to...", "the largest effect") are allowed only for one named outcome and only if the Key numbers block confirms them (bad: "the only registered arm to harm performance"; good: "the only arm that lowered accuracy"). When an effect is negative, write the CI of the effect itself, e.g. −3.9 points (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]), never a flipped-sign interval. Use the "Key numbers" block for the figures. Write "p < 0.001" for any p-value below 0.001, never "p = 0.000".

Abstract: one paragraph, 120 to 170 words, in the order a journal abstract uses: the question, the design and sample in one sentence, the main results with their numbers, and one sentence of caveat. It must stand alone when shared without the rest of the report.

Length: abstract ≤ 170 words; design_notes ≤ 120 words; each result note ≤ 110 words; each exploratory note ≤ 60 words; limitations ≤ 150 words.

- E1: Planned H1 estimates restricted to finished responses — Restricting to finished responses (dropping 7.5% of rows) left all 32 arm estimates unchanged in pattern (correlation 1.000 with the original), with 5 arms significant at p<0.05 both before and after and a median standard-error ratio of 1.00. - E2: Heterogeneity of planned H1 arm effects by Republican identification — Only 1 of 32 arm-by-Republican interaction estimates has p<0.05, which is about the rate expected by chance at the 5% level, so there is no clear partisan heterogeneity in the planned arm effects. [table results/E2_party_interaction.csv]

## Literature note
The retrieved literature on the hypothesis is thin. Van Bavel et al. (2020) argue that social and behavioural science should inform the COVID-19 pandemic response, which gives general backing to testing whether brief messages can shape public attitudes toward science. Ecker et al. (2022) review the psychological drivers of misinformation belief and its resistance to correction, which bears on whether any single message can move trust in science relative to a pure control. Berinsky et al. (2012) assess the internal and external validity of experiments run on Amazon Mechanical Turk, a relevant reference for an online randomised design. The main tension is between the expectation that messages can shift trust and Ecker et al.'s account of how resistant beliefs are to correction. Van Bavel et al. take the policy case for behavioural interventions as given, while Ecker et al. suggest that changing entrenched beliefs is hard. A design with 32 messages against a pure control can test whether any message departs from control, which speaks directly to this disagreement. Berinsky et al.'s validity concerns mean that any such effects would need to be read with the sample's limits in mind.

## Abstract

Can brief, student-designed messages raise trust in science? We ran a registered online survey experiment with US adults recruited through Lucid, randomly assigning respondents to one of 32 messages (videos, texts, memes, posters and infographics) or a pure control that only asked them to continue. Of 11,519 raw responses, 8,572 were analysed. Trust in science was measured after treatment on a scale where the control mean was 3.685. One video, 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?', lowered trust by 0.171 points (95% CI [−0.262, −0.080], p = 0.0002), and the 'Powers of Ten' clip lowered it by 0.104 points. Three videos raised trust by roughly 0.06 points each: the peer-review video and two student-made videos. For the other arms the results were inconclusive; their intervals were wide and do not rule out small effects. Tests were uncorrected for multiplicity and several arms were small, so the modest findings should be read cautiously.

<!-- fd:section id=findings -->
## Key findings

- Most of the 32 messages were inconclusive against the pure control on trust in science; the few with uncorrected p < 0.05 moved it by small amounts.
- Registered: the 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?' video lowered trust in science by 0.171 scale points (95% CI [−0.262, −0.080], p < 0.001).
- Registered: three videos raised trust in science by about 0.06 scale points each, including both student-made videos (e.g. Science through the day, 95% CI [0.016, 0.111]).
- Caveat: 32 uncorrected two-sided tests, several arms with about 120 people, and effects near the threshold mean the smaller findings may be chance.

### E2. Heterogeneity of planned H1 arm effects by Republican identification

Partisanship is the most likely source of variation in trust in science, so the planned arm contrasts are checked for differences between Republicans and non-Republicans. The planned treatment-versus-control comparisons were re-estimated with an interaction between each arm and a 0/1 indicator of Republican identification, and the interaction estimates were tabulated.

**Finding.** Only 1 of 32 arm-by-Republican interaction estimates has p<0.05, which is about the rate expected by chance at the 5% level, so there is no clear partisan heterogeneity in the planned arm effects.

Exploratory, unreviewed code: one arm-by-Republican-identification interaction was significant at p < 0.05, and the others were imprecise. This does not establish whether partisan differences exist.

<!-- fd:section id=related -->
## Related work

The retrieved literature on the hypothesis is thin. Van Bavel et al. (2020) argue that social and behavioural science should inform the COVID-19 pandemic response, which gives general backing to testing whether brief messages can shape public attitudes toward science. Ecker et al. (2022) review the psychological drivers of misinformation belief and its resistance to correction, which bears on whether any single message can move trust in science relative to a pure control. Berinsky et al. (2012) assess the internal and external validity of experiments run on Amazon Mechanical Turk, a relevant reference for an online randomised design. The main tension is between the expectation that messages can shift trust and Ecker et al.'s account of how resistant beliefs are to correction. Van Bavel et al. take the policy case for behavioural interventions as given, while Ecker et al. suggest that changing entrenched beliefs is hard. A design with 32 messages against a pure control can test whether any message departs from control, which speaks directly to this disagreement. Berinsky et al.'s validity concerns mean that any such effects would need to be read with the sample's limits in mind.

Retrieved works (OpenAlex; queries: trust in science persuasive messages experiment; science messaging intervention improves trust vaccine; trust in science interventions null effects; backfire effect corrective messages science skepticism; adaptive multi-arm bandit survey experiment messaging):

- Jay Joseph Van Bavel, Katherine Baicker, Paulo S. Boggio, Valerio Capraro (2020). Using social and behavioural science to support COVID-19 pandemic response. Nature Human Behaviour. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-020-0884-z
- Adam J. Berinsky, Gregory A. Huber, Gabriel S. Lenz (2012). Evaluating Online Labor Markets for Experimental Research: Amazon.com's Mechanical Turk. Political Analysis. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpr057
- Ullrich K. H. Ecker, Stephan Lewandowsky, John Cook, Philipp Schmid (2022). The psychological drivers of misinformation belief and its resistance to correction. Nature Reviews Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1038/s44159-021-00006-y

<!-- fd:section id=limitations -->
## Limitations

Thirty-two two-sided tests were run without correction for multiplicity, so some of the five effects with p < 0.05 may be false positives, especially those with p near 0.03. Adaptive assignment left some arms with only about 120 respondents, giving wide intervals. The effects are small, at most about 0.17 points on the trust scale, and only trust measured right after exposure is observed, so durability is unknown. Lucid is an online panel, so results may not generalise beyond it. Several messages differ in format, length and content, so the design cannot say which feature drives an effect.

messages.content:
You write the narrative sections of a short research report on an unpublished survey experiment, for a reader who knows social science but has not seen the study. You receive the hypotheses with their tags (registered / deviation / exploratory), the result tables, exploratory findings, and a literature note. The report skeleton already prints the model formulas, the full tables, a key-findings table and the figures; your job is the prose around them.

Voice: a careful colleague explaining the study to a peer, not a form being filled in. Vary sentence openings; do not begin the summary and the design notes the same way; do not restate the hypothesis sentence that already sits under each heading; say "significant" once per section at most and otherwise let the interval speak.

Style:
- Plain, legible English. Short paragraphs (2-4 sentences). One idea per sentence. Lead with what was found, then how.
- Describe the sample exactly as design.population.description says when it is given (e.g. 'US Latino adults', not 'US adults'); never widen it.
- Refer to arms and outcomes by their labels (e.g. "Automated Flagging", "total accuracy"), never by codes or column names. Do not paste formulas, column names, variable codes or file paths into prose; they are shown separately.
- For an outcome on a 0-1 proportion scale, state effects in percentage points ("4.4 points higher", from +0.044) and give the raw estimate once in parentheses if useful. Give a 95% CI for each effect you name.
- Name the significant effects with their CI and p-value; summarise the rest in one sentence ("the other eight arms were within about ±3 points of control and not distinguishable from it"). Do not list every arm's numbers.
- Numbers must come from the tables. Never add results that are not in the tables.
- A non-significant estimate is inconclusive, not evidence of no effect. Never write "had no effect", "did not change" or "neither improved nor harmed"; say it was not distinguishable from zero and give the CI.
- Cite the p-value that matches the hypothesis (`p_directional`, one-sided for a stated direction, when present) and say whether it is one- or two-sided, once.
- Mention the sample flow once, in the design notes: raw N, analysis N, and any rows dropped for missing values (`n_eligible` vs model `n`), plus the control-group size.
- If the plan was not pre-registered (registration status "none"), say once, plainly, that every test is post hoc, and never call an analysis "registered" or "pre-specified". If an analysis carries a deviation tag, say in one sentence what changed and why it matters (or does not).
- Exploratory results (E1, E2, ...) come from model-written code that nobody has reviewed. Report them only in their own section and in at most one takeaway, introduced as exploratory. Never let an exploratory result overturn, qualify or cast doubt on a registered result in the abstract or the registered results; if an exploratory check disagrees with a registered estimate, say in the exploratory section that the two disagree and that the check is unreviewed.
- Do not overclaim: p-values near the threshold, small arms and many uncorrected tests all deserve a hedge, stated once.
- No headings, no bullet lists, no bold, no markdown tables inside your sections; plain paragraphs only.

Takeaways: 3 to 5 bullets for a reader who will read nothing else. Each is one or two plain sentences, at most 30 words, with one number at most (the effect in natural units with its CI or p-value). The first bullet answers the research question; the middle ones give the findings that matter, saying "registered" or "exploratory" where it changes the reading; the last gives the main caveat (multiple uncorrected tests, small arms, post hoc). No codes, no column names, no lists of every arm. Every claim names its outcome. Words like "performance", "outcomes" or "anything" are not outcomes. Superlatives ("the only arm to...", "the largest effect") are allowed only for one named outcome and only if the Key numbers block confirms them (bad: "the only registered arm to harm performance"; good: "the only arm that lowered accuracy"). When an effect is negative, write the CI of the effect itself, e.g. −3.9 points (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]), never a flipped-sign interval. Use the "Key numbers" block for the figures. Write "p < 0.001" for any p-value below 0.001, never "p = 0.000".

Abstract: one paragraph, 120 to 170 words, in the order a journal abstract uses: the question, the design and sample in one sentence, the main results with their numbers, and one sentence of caveat. It must stand alone when shared without the rest of the report.

Length: abstract ≤ 170 words; design_notes ≤ 120 words; each result note ≤ 110 words; each exploratory note ≤ 60 words; limitations ≤ 150 words.

## Exploratory
- E1: Planned H1 estimates restricted to finished responses — Restricting to finished responses (dropping 7.5% of rows) left all 32 arm estimates unchanged in pattern (correlation 1.000 with the original), with 5 arms significant at p<0.05 both before and after and a median standard-error ratio of 1.00. [table results/E1_finished_only.csv]
- E2: Heterogeneity of planned H1 arm effects by Republican identification — Only 1 of 32 arm-by-Republican interaction estimates has p<0.05, which is about the rate expected by chance at the 5% level, so there is no clear partisan heterogeneity in the planned arm effects. [table results/E2_party_interaction.csv]

## Literature note
The retrieved literature on the hypothesis is thin. Van Bavel et al. (2020) argue that social and behavioural science should inform the COVID-19 pandemic response, which gives general backing to testing whether brief messages can shape public attitudes toward science. Ecker et al. (2022) review the psychological drivers of misinformation belief and its resistance to correction, which bears on whether any single message can move trust in science relative to a pure control. Berinsky et al. (2012) assess the internal and external validity of experiments run on Amazon Mechanical Turk, a relevant reference for an online randomised design. The main tension is between the expectation that messages can shift trust and Ecker et al.'s account of how resistant beliefs are to correction. Van Bavel et al. take the policy case for behavioural interventions as given, while Ecker et al. suggest that changing entrenched beliefs is hard. A design with 32 messages against a pure control can test whether any message departs from control, which speaks directly to this disagreement. Berinsky et al.'s validity concerns mean that any such effects would need to be read with the sample's limits in mind.

<!-- fd:section id=abstract -->
## Abstract

Can brief, student-designed messages raise trust in science? We ran a registered online survey experiment with US adults recruited through Lucid, randomly assigning respondents to one of 32 messages (videos, texts, memes, posters and infographics) or a pure control that only asked them to continue. Of 11,519 raw responses, 8,572 were analysed. Trust in science was measured after treatment on a scale where the control mean was 3.685. One video, 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?', lowered trust by 0.171 points (95% CI [−0.262, −0.080], p < 0.001), and the 'Powers of Ten' clip lowered it by 0.104 points. Three videos raised trust by roughly 0.06 points each: the peer-review video and two student-made videos. For the other arms the results were inconclusive; their intervals were wide and do not rule out small effects. Tests were uncorrected for multiplicity and several arms were small, so the modest findings should be read cautiously.

<!-- fd:section id=findings -->
## Key findings

- Most of the 32 messages were inconclusive against the pure control on trust in science; the few with uncorrected p < 0.05 moved it by small amounts.
- Registered: the 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?' video lowered trust in science by 0.171 scale points (95% CI [−0.262, −0.080], p < 0.001).
- Registered: three videos raised trust in science by about 0.06 scale points each, including both student-made videos (e.g. Science through the day, 95% CI [0.016, 0.111]).
- Caveat: 32 uncorrected two-sided tests, several arms with about 120 people, and effects near the threshold mean the smaller findings may be chance.

<!-- fd:hyp id=H1 tag=registered outcome=post_trust -->
### H1. Trust in science after treatment

*Registered: the effect of each of the 32 messages on trust in science, relative to the pure control.*  
*Pre-registered.*

![H1: effect by arm](figures/H1_arms.png)

Five of the 32 messages had uncorrected two-sided p < 0.05. The 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?' video lowered trust by 0.171 points (95% CI [−0.262, −0.080], p < 0.001), and the 'Powers of Ten' clip by 0.104 points (95% CI [−0.184, −0.024], p = 0.010). Three videos raised it by about 0.06 points: Science through the day (95% CI [0.016, 0.111], p = 0.009), Science in everyday life (95% CI [0.014, 0.112], p = 0.012) and the peer-review video (95% CI [0.005, 0.123], p = 0.034). The remaining arms had intervals including zero, so they are inconclusive rather than shown to be ineffective. With 32 uncorrected tests, the p-values near 0.03 deserve particular caution.

## Exploratory analyses

*Everything in this section is exploratory and was not pre-registered.*

<!-- fd:hyp id=E1 tag=exploratory kind=pipeline -->
### E1. Planned H1 estimates restricted to finished responses

Unfinished responses make up a sizeable share of the sample, so the planned arm contrasts are re-estimated on completed surveys to check that the registered pattern does not depend on partial responses. The planned treatment-versus-control comparisons on trust in science were re-estimated with the same specification on the subset of respondents who finished the survey, and the arm estimates and standard errors were set side by side with the original ones.

**Finding.** Restricting to finished responses (dropping 7.5% of rows) left all 32 arm estimates unchanged in pattern (correlation 1.000 with the original), with 5 arms significant at p<0.05 both before and after and a median standard-error ratio of 1.00.

Exploratory, unreviewed code: the finished-only subset equals the analysed sample (7,803 rows in both), so the check is uninformative about whether incomplete responses matter.

<!-- fd:hyp id=E2 tag=exploratory kind=pipeline -->
### E2. Heterogeneity of planned H1 arm effects by Republican identification

Partisanship is the most likely source of variation in trust in science, so the planned arm contrasts are checked for differences between Republicans and non-Republicans. The planned treatment-versus-control comparisons were re-estimated with an interaction between each arm and a 0/1 indicator of Republican identification, and the interaction estimates were tabulated.

**Finding.** Only 1 of 32 arm-by-Republican interaction estimates has p<0.05, which is about the rate expected by chance at the 5% level, so there is no clear partisan heterogeneity in the planned arm effects.

Exploratory, unreviewed code: one arm-by-Republican-identification interaction was significant at p < 0.05, and the others were imprecise. Partisan differences are therefore not established.

## Related work

The retrieved literature on the hypothesis is thin. Van Bavel et al. (2020) argue that social and behavioural science should inform the COVID-19 pandemic response, which gives general backing to testing whether brief messages can shape public attitudes toward science. Ecker et al. (2022) review the psychological drivers of misinformation belief and its resistance to correction, which bears on whether any single message can move trust in science relative to a pure control. Berinsky et al. (2012) assess the internal and external validity of experiments run on Amazon Mechanical Turk, a relevant reference for an online randomised design. The main tension is between the expectation that messages can shift trust and Ecker et al.'s account of how resistant beliefs are to correction. Van Bavel et al. take the policy case for behavioural interventions as given, while Ecker et al. suggest that changing entrenched beliefs is hard. A design with 32 messages against a pure control can test whether any message departs from control, which speaks directly to this disagreement. Berinsky et al.'s validity concerns mean that any such effects would need to be read with the sample's limits in mind.

Retrieved works (OpenAlex; queries: trust in science persuasive messages experiment; science messaging intervention improves trust vaccine; trust in science interventions null effects; backfire effect corrective messages science skepticism; adaptive multi-arm bandit survey experiment messaging):

- Jay Joseph Van Bavel, Katherine Baicker, Paulo S. Boggio, Valerio Capraro (2020). Using social and behavioural science to support COVID-19 pandemic response. Nature Human Behaviour. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-020-0884-z
- Adam J. Berinsky, Gregory A. Huber, Gabriel S. Lenz (2012). Evaluating Online Labor Markets for Experimental Research: Amazon.com's Mechanical Turk. Political Analysis. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpr057
- Ullrich K. H. Ecker, Stephan Lewandowsky, John Cook, Philipp Schmid (2022). The psychological drivers of misinformation belief and its resistance to correction. Nature Reviews Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1038/s44159-021-00006-y

## Limitations

Thirty-two two-sided tests were run without correction for multiplicity, so some of the five effects with p < 0.05 may be false positives, especially those with p near 0.03. Adaptive assignment left some arms with only about 120 respondents, giving wide intervals. The effects are small, at most about 0.17 points on the trust scale, and only trust measured right after exposure is observed, so durability is unknown. Lucid is an online panel, so results may not generalise beyond it. Several messages differ in format, length and content, so the design cannot say which feature drives an effect.

## Abstract

Can brief, student-designed messages raise trust in science? We ran a registered online survey experiment with US adults recruited through Lucid, randomly assigning respondents to one of 32 messages (videos, texts, memes, posters and infographics) or a pure control that only asked them to continue. Of 11,519 raw responses, 8,572 were analysed. Trust in science was measured after treatment on a scale where the control mean was 3.685. One video, 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?', lowered trust by 0.171 points (95% CI [−0.262, −0.080], p < 0.001), and the 'Powers of Ten' clip lowered it by 0.104 points. Three videos raised trust by roughly 0.06 points each: the peer-review video and two student-made videos. For the other arms the results were inconclusive; their intervals were wide and do not rule out small effects. Tests were uncorrected for multiplicity and several arms were small, so the modest findings should be read cautiously.

<!-- fd:section id=findings -->
## Key findings

- Most of the 32 messages were inconclusive against the pure control on trust in science; the few with uncorrected p < 0.05 moved it by small amounts.
- Registered: the 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?' video lowered trust in science by 0.171 scale points (95% CI [−0.262, −0.080], p < 0.001).
- Registered: three videos raised trust in science by about 0.06 scale points each, including both student-made videos (e.g. Science through the day, 95% CI [0.016, 0.111]).
- Caveat: 32 uncorrected two-sided tests, several arms with about 120 people, and effects near the threshold mean the smaller findings may be chance.

### H1. Trust in science after treatment

*Registered: the effect of each of the 32 messages on trust in science, relative to the pure control.*  
*Pre-registered.*

![H1: effect by arm](figures/H1_arms.png)

Five of the 32 messages had uncorrected two-sided p < 0.05. The 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?' video lowered trust by 0.171 points (95% CI [−0.262, −0.080], p < 0.001), and the 'Powers of Ten' clip by 0.104 points (95% CI [−0.184, −0.024], p = 0.010). Three videos raised it by about 0.06 points: Science through the day (95% CI [0.016, 0.111], p = 0.009), Science in everyday life (95% CI [0.014, 0.112], p = 0.012) and the peer-review video (95% CI [0.005, 0.123], p = 0.034). The remaining arms had intervals including zero, so they are inconclusive rather than shown to be ineffective. With 32 uncorrected tests, the p-values near 0.03 deserve particular caution.

### E1. Planned H1 estimates restricted to finished responses

Unfinished responses make up a sizeable share of the sample, so the planned arm contrasts are re-estimated on completed surveys to check that the registered pattern does not depend on partial responses. The planned treatment-versus-control comparisons on trust in science were re-estimated with the same specification on the subset of respondents who finished the survey, and the arm estimates and standard errors were set side by side with the original ones.

**Finding.** Restricting to finished responses (dropping 7.5% of rows) left all 32 arm estimates unchanged in pattern (correlation 1.000 with the original), with 5 arms significant at p<0.05 both before and after and a median standard-error ratio of 1.00.

Exploratory, unreviewed code: the finished-only subset equals the analysed sample (7,803 rows in both), so the check is uninformative about whether incomplete responses matter.

### E2. Heterogeneity of planned H1 arm effects by Republican identification

Partisanship is the most likely source of variation in trust in science, so the planned arm contrasts are checked for differences between Republicans and non-Republicans. The planned treatment-versus-control comparisons were re-estimated with an interaction between each arm and a 0/1 indicator of Republican identification, and the interaction estimates were tabulated.

**Finding.** Only 1 of 32 arm-by-Republican interaction estimates has p<0.05, which is about the rate expected by chance at the 5% level, so there is no clear partisan heterogeneity in the planned arm effects.

Exploratory, unreviewed code: one arm-by-Republican-identification interaction was significant at p < 0.05, and the others were imprecise. Partisan differences are therefore not established.

<!-- fd:section id=related -->
## Related work

The retrieved literature on the hypothesis is thin. Van Bavel et al. (2020) argue that social and behavioural science should inform the COVID-19 pandemic response, which gives general backing to testing whether brief messages can shape public attitudes toward science. Ecker et al. (2022) review the psychological drivers of misinformation belief and its resistance to correction, which bears on whether any single message can move trust in science relative to a pure control. Berinsky et al. (2012) assess the internal and external validity of experiments run on Amazon Mechanical Turk, a relevant reference for an online randomised design. The main tension is between the expectation that messages can shift trust and Ecker et al.'s account of how resistant beliefs are to correction. Van Bavel et al. take the policy case for behavioural interventions as given, while Ecker et al. suggest that changing entrenched beliefs is hard. A design with 32 messages against a pure control can test whether any message departs from control, which speaks directly to this disagreement. Berinsky et al.'s validity concerns mean that any such effects would need to be read with the sample's limits in mind.

Retrieved works (OpenAlex; queries: trust in science persuasive messages experiment; science messaging intervention improves trust vaccine; trust in science interventions null effects; backfire effect corrective messages science skepticism; adaptive multi-arm bandit survey experiment messaging):

- Jay Joseph Van Bavel, Katherine Baicker, Paulo S. Boggio, Valerio Capraro (2020). Using social and behavioural science to support COVID-19 pandemic response. Nature Human Behaviour. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-020-0884-z
- Adam J. Berinsky, Gregory A. Huber, Gabriel S. Lenz (2012). Evaluating Online Labor Markets for Experimental Research: Amazon.com's Mechanical Turk. Political Analysis. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpr057
- Ullrich K. H. Ecker, Stephan Lewandowsky, John Cook, Philipp Schmid (2022). The psychological drivers of misinformation belief and its resistance to correction. Nature Reviews Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1038/s44159-021-00006-y

<!-- fd:section id=limitations -->
## Limitations

Thirty-two two-sided tests were run without correction for multiplicity, so some of the five effects with p < 0.05 may be false positives, especially those with p near 0.03. Adaptive assignment left some arms with only about 120 respondents, giving wide intervals. The effects are small, at most about 0.17 points on the trust scale, and only trust measured right after exposure is observed, so durability is unknown. Lucid is an online panel, so results may not generalise beyond it. Several messages differ in format, length and content, so the design cannot say which feature drives an effect.

messages.content:
You design ONE follow-up survey experiment that extends a finished study. You see the study's abstract, key results and limitations, its design, and the questions of its original survey. You never see respondent data.

Hand the design over with record_result(key="proposal", value=<object>, final=true). Do not write prose outside the object.

The object is an ExtensionProposal:
{"id": the kind given in the task, "kind": "mechanism"|"boundary"|"alternative", "addresses": [ids of unresolved reviewer questions this design answers, e.g. "U1"; may be empty], "title": str, "rationale": 2-3 sentences tying the extension to a specific result or limitation of the source study (cite numbers from the results), "contribution": one sentence, "limitations": [str],
 "design": {"title", "overview", "hypothesis", "primaryOutcome", "comparison", "population", "conditions": [{"id","title","description","nodeId"}], "blocks": [{"id","title","questions": [Question]}], "flow": [FlowNode], "roots": [ids], "assumptions": [str], "unresolved": [str], "evidence": [{"id","title","url","claim","excerpt","origin": "supplied"}]}}

Kinds: "mechanism" tests WHY the source effect (or null) happened; "boundary" tests WHERE it holds (a population, stimulus or context the source did not cover); "alternative" tests a rival explanation or a different intervention for the same outcome.

Design rules (they are checked by a validator; violations are sent back to you):
Produce a complete, concise standalone English survey experiment using the exact schema. Every collecting question needs a unique readable tag. IDs start with letters and contain letters/numbers/underscores. MC choices have stable local IDs, text, numeric recode strings. Matrix rows are statements and choices are scale points. Use empty arrays/strings for irrelevant fields. DB is participant-facing descriptive text. Do not include executable HTML or code. Flow is a flat list with unique IDs, and "roots" lists the top-level node ids in order; child references form a tree. block nodes reference blocks; group nodes contain sequences; randomizer nodes select exactly one equally allocated child arm. Group each arm with an embedded field recording the condition plus its treatment block: randomizer r1 has children [arm_a, arm_b]; arm_a is a group whose children are [set_a, treat_a]; set_a is an embedded node with field "condition" and value "a"; treat_a is a block node. Each condition's nodeId is the group (arm_a), never the embedded node, the block, or the randomizer. block, embedded and end nodes have empty children. A branch after consent is a sibling of the consent block, not its child. Every FlowNode has all fields: id, type, label, children, blockId, field, value, questionId, choiceId, operator ("equals" when unused); unused string fields are "". Every Question has all fields: id, type, text, tag, multiple, required, choices, rows, sourceQuestionId. Ask consent before treatment and route non-consent to an end node through a branch on the consent MC question (operator "selected"). The full instrument includes consent, every treatment, the outcome measures and a debrief. Stimuli that are media live in an embedded node piped into a DB question with {{ed:field}}: [IMAGE: what the image shows] for a still image, [VIDEO: what the clip shows and its length] for a clip the research team hosts. Use one embedded node per stimulus (field names like post1, post2); the DB question text pipes it, e.g. "{{ed:post1}}", and the outcome question for that post follows it. Every {{ed:field}} used in question text must be set by an embedded node earlier in the flow. NEVER put [RESEARCHER INPUT REQUIRED], TBD, TODO or placeholders in question text: the validator rejects the whole design. Anything only the research team can supply (the actual media files, IRB numbers, compensation) goes in design.unresolved as a plain sentence, and the participant wording stays complete. Record practical judgment calls (sample size with rationale, platform, compensation) in design.assumptions.

Grounding rules:
- Reuse the source survey's outcome questions verbatim where they fit, with sourceQuestionId set to their QSF id (e.g. "QID12"); use "" for new questions. Only ids listed under "Source survey questions" are valid.
- evidence: cite only the allowed sources listed in the task, by their exact url; origin "supplied"; excerpt may be "".
- Two to four arms. Keep it short enough for a 10-minute survey.

Write the 'mechanism'-type extension specified in the brief below.

## Brief (design exactly this; use id 'advance_design')
Type: advance_design (survey_experiment). Title: Replicating the short student videos with a delayed follow-up and a behavioural outcome
Question: Do short everyday-science student videos raise trust in science, and does the effect persist a week later and carry over to a behavioural choice?
Why this follow-up fixes what held the source study back: Addresses power and measurement. It concentrates the sample on the two best-supported arms plus the peer-review video, tests them against control in a confirmatory design, and adds a delayed and a behavioural outcome.
Design sketch: Four arms: Science through the day, Science in everyday life, the peer-review video, and a pure control. Fixed equal allocation, with pre-treatment trust measured. Outcomes are immediate trust, trust at 7 days, and a behavioural choice (such as donating a bonus to a science organisation or choosing a science-based news article). Analysis is registered, with Holm correction across the three treatment contrasts.
Power target: about 4000 per arm to detect 0.03 at 80% power (Observed effect of about 0.063 (SE 0.025 at n=853-921). The power table was empty, so the sample size is a back-of-envelope estimate of about 1,000 per arm for 80% power at 0.063. 4,000 per arm gives headroom to detect effects of about half that size and for attrition in the delayed wave.); record it in design.assumptions
Debate the design must discriminate between (D1: Can brief messages move trust in science?): (a) Brief, well-designed messages and behavioural interventions can shift public attitudes toward science. versus (b) Entrenched beliefs resist correction, so single brief messages leave trust largely unchanged relative to control.. The source study says: The evidence leans toward position b. Most of the 32 messages are inconclusive, and the significant effects are at most 0.06 points up and 0.17 down. Small positive shifts from short student videos cannot be ruled out, but they are not robust to multiplicity.

## Source study
Title: Can Trust in Science Be Improved? An Adaptive Experiment Testing Student-Designed Messages

Abstract: Can brief, student-designed messages raise trust in science? We ran a registered online survey experiment with US adults recruited through Lucid, randomly assigning respondents to one of 32 messages (videos, texts, memes, posters and infographics) or a pure control that only asked them to continue. Of 11,519 raw responses, 8,572 were analysed. Trust in science was measured after treatment on a scale where the control mean was 3.685. One video, 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?', lowered trust by 0.171 points (95% CI [−0.262, −0.080], p < 0.001), and the 'Powers of Ten' clip lowered it by 0.104 points. Three videos raised trust by roughly 0.06 points each: the peer-review video and two student-made videos. For the other arms the results were inconclusive; their intervals were wide and do not rule out small effects. Tests were uncorrected for multiplicity and several arms were small, so the modest findings should be read cautiously.

Key findings:
- Most of the 32 messages were inconclusive against the pure control on trust in science; the few with uncorrected p < 0.05 moved it by small amounts.
- Registered: the 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?' video lowered trust in science by 0.171 scale points (95% CI [−0.262, −0.080], p < 0.001).
- Registered: three videos raised trust in science by about 0.06 scale points each, including both student-made videos (e.g. Science through the day, 95% CI [0.016, 0.111]).
- Caveat: 32 uncorrected two-sided tests, several arms with about 120 people, and effects near the threshold mean the smaller findings may be chance.

Limitations: Thirty-two two-sided tests were run without correction for multiplicity, so some of the five effects with p < 0.05 may be false positives, especially those with p near 0.03. Adaptive assignment left some arms with only about 120 respondents, giving wide intervals. The effects are small, at most about 0.17 points on the trust scale, and only trust measured right after exposure is observed, so durability is unknown. Lucid is an online panel, so results may not generalise beyond it. Several messages differ in format, length and content, so the design cannot say which feature drives an effect.

value.title: Replicating the short student videos with a delayed follow-up and a behavioural outcome
value.rationale: In the source study, Science through the day (about 0.06, SE 0.025) and Science in everyday life (0.063, SE 0.025) were near the threshold among 32 uncorrected tests. The peer-review video had 0.064 (p=0.034). Only immediate trust was measured, so durability and behavioural carry-over are unknown. This confirmatory test concentrates the sample on those three videos plus control and adds a 7-day and a behavioural outcome.
value.contribution: Provides a Holm-corrected confirmatory test of whether short science videos raise trust, whether any effect lasts 7 days, and whether it changes a behavioural choice.
limitations: Behavioural choice is a hypothetical or low-stakes proxy.
Attrition in the delayed wave may be differential by arm.
Videos differ in content and format, so the design cannot isolate which feature matters.
Online panel sample may not generalise.

design.title: Short student videos: confirmatory test with 7-day follow-up and behavioural choice
design.overview: US adults complete pre-treatment trust items, are randomised to one of three videos or a control page, then report immediate trust and make a behavioural choice. A week later they complete trust again.
design.hypothesis: Each video raises immediate trust relative to control (position a). Under position b, contrasts are near zero after Holm correction. Effects at 7 days are smaller than or equal to immediate effects.
design.primaryOutcome: Immediate post-treatment trust in science (mean of 6 items, items 4-6 reverse-coded), with 7-day trust and the behavioural choice as secondary outcomes.
design.comparison: Each of the three videos against control, with Holm correction across the three contrasts, covariate-adjusted for pre-treatment trust.
design.population: US adults from an online panel such as Lucid, quota-matched to the adult population.
